pages.transcription:
Hotel Paysandú, Rio 29. Sept. 1940
letter 8 from Rio
Dear Manfred and Hannah, you write that you want long letters — alas, it
is the only thing we can do for you. I am ashamed to say that all is perfect
here, the climat delicious (now in winter time) the people wonderful and all sym-
pathies on the side of England. We just came back from the interior, where we
were invited by the Governor of the province Minas Geraes; we were taken to the
capital in an a plane, had an autocar with a charming secretary of the ministry
all the time at our disposition and were brought back in two days auto-travelling
through the country. By that we have seen a lot and the real life of Brasil. Next
week we will go somewhere in the mountains to have a rest {before we leave} — we are not tired,
not in the least, but I want to do some {afterwards} here we are bombarded with
invitations, interviews and I am looking forward for a few days without speaking
in five languages to two hundred people and not to have our picture in the paper.
If it would be for Lotte, we would not leave at all Brasil, she is very changed
and is restoring me every moment in her exalted way with exclamations. Is it
not marvellous and so on and ? have married her just because she has been formerly
so discret, but I have to do my duty and we will leave about the 22 October.
I have two lectures in Montevideo and will give two at Buenos-Aires and two
in the universities of Cordoba and Rosario. They had made me a programme of
six lectures in Buenos Aires, but I have enough. The lectures are well paid and
we can make easily our living from it, so I do not want to make a profession
out of it. Later on I should go to Chile and Venezuela and Cuba, I have from
everywhere urgent offers, I think however I will not accept them and you will
understand it if you look on the map, what enormous distances that means.
And all the receptions in all these little countries, the noisy publicity are against
my conception of life. It is good to know, that I could make my living for
months and months going around as a lecturer but we prefere a more quiet way
and it is impossible to write in midst of such travelling, thanks God, I am not
gready neither for money nor for honours. By the way, please dispose of my
accounts for you and your family as it were yours and I would be grateful
if you would sent to friends like Friedental or Pleinher something to relieve
her situation, I feel somewhat guilty that I have here all honours and a decent
living through my work while you are disturbed in your profession and have gracious
days and nights. Please believe me that I do not care at all for the house and the
property; we are all reduced to the minimum of what men can ask from life —
life itself and this is already much in these days. And now to Eva. I am sure she
My former wife could come to Lisbon and is already on the way overseas, and how many are
still in France. Even here we get letters and telegrams from all sides.
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Stefan Zweig. Der Text am linken Rand ist vertikal geschrieben. Die Tinte ist violett.

pages.transcription:
will feel all right at Salmons and please dont forget that we shall be in three
months ourselves at Newyork and I hope you know that we are reliable and that
Eva will have a second mother and a good uncle. About her musiclessons I wrote to
her, You may imagine how gladly surprised I was to hear from her progress. So you may
be without any worries about her and about us. Please send us often cables, it has
not sense to be on your side parsimonious and perhaps you can send them even
with paid answer so that you may be sure that we are always able to give you notice
about our whereabouts. Dear Hannah and Manfred, I know it is a hard moral task for
you not to envy us who can continue our work quietly and in a beautiful surround-
ing but I feel that your good wishes are with us as ours are always with you. Stefan
postal address from now on, even when we have left Brasil:
Dear Hanna and Manfred, c/o editora GUANABARA, 132 Rua Ouvidor, Rio de Janeiro
Today we got your and Mama's letter of the 12th Sept.
after two weeks without news except the cable about Eva's arrival. Please do
not forget that I wait just as impatiently for your letters as you for ours and
write regularly and as often as possible, if only a few lines. If I cannot be
with you, I want at least to know everything about you and our friends. I hope
you had a few days rest in Bath. We had a letter from Ingram yesterday and
write him and Mr. Orchard by airmail today. I am glad that you can rely upon
their advise and help if necessary. Has Lorle been alone with Ursel in the house
all the time, except for Griffith? I was sorry to hear that Mr. Miller is ill,
I hope he will recover again, he belongs to my memory of the house just as much
as you and the children and Marta. Is Alice still in Baker Street? I hope the
affidavit for Heiner has arrived by now. Mr. Landau assured me that it had been
cabbed but he had himself no detailed news about it, as he was travelling about
and got no letters himself but only cables. - I cannot tell you how glad I
was that you cabled me Eva's arrival. I got your cable Sunday afternoon and I
read the news about the ship disaster in the Atlantic about an hour before
Salmon's cable arrived. What a shock it must have been for you and what a
relief that she was not only on the other ship but already safely arrived. I
have not yet a letter from her, but I suppose it is on the way. I wrote her
last week and am writing her again today so that she does not feel all alone,
even though I feel sure that she is already on the best of terms with Mr. and
Mrs. Salmon. She will just have arrived in time for the new term in school and
Mr. Salmon assured me that there were excellent public schools in New Rochelle,
and that they knew plenty of children in the neighbourhood. My sister-in-law
was already in touch with Mrs. Salmon before Eva's arrival and will certainly
have visited her by now, and I suppose Rose will go to see her too, so that I
will have reports from them soon. - I hope that you are all in good health and
that you are not too much exhausted by the lack of sleep and the continous
excitements. I am glad that you have a good shelter at last and that you are
even able to sleep there. Has Manfred to go out a lot or has his practice gone
down with the latest events? I could also imagine that he has a lot more to do
and I only hope that he has not to go out during an attack. We think of you more
often than you imagine and the people here too are very sympathetic to the cause
of England. - From ourselves I can only repeat that we have a much too good
time, that everybody is extremely nice and that the only drawback is that they
are even too nice. We have so many invitations and the newspapers are so in-
terested in what Stefan does that we consider going to a small place in the
mountains nearby at the end of this week so that Stefan can work quietly at
least for a few days and that our brains can have a rest from the continual
change of faces before us and of the change of languages in the conversation.
Last week we have been in the province of Minas, as Stefan wrote, and it was
very interesting to travel through the country.
Kindest regards to you all, Lotte
